I’ve farmed this 2.6 mu in Quzhou for 40 years. My wife and I are the only ones at home now, so I can’t afford to overwork myself, but I know this soil like the back of my hand. The land is good loam, and my well has never let me down. I’ll stick with the wheat-maize rotation I’ve always done—it’s what this soil is made for.

For winter wheat, I’ll sow my usual improved variety in October after a quick rotary tillage. I trust this seed; it’s never failed me. I’ll apply about 15 kg of nitrogen, 6 kg of phosphorus, and 4 kg of potassium per mu—enough to feed the crop without wasting money. I’ll irrigate three times: once after sowing to help it settle, once at jointing when the wheat is thirsty, and once during grain filling to plump the kernels. Two pesticide sprays will do—one for weeds and another if I see aphids or rust.

Come June, right after the wheat harvest, I’ll rotary till again and plant hybrid maize seed. Maize needs plenty of nitrogen, so I’ll give it 16 kg per mu, plus 5 kg phosphorus and 4 kg potassium. I’ll irrigate twice: once if June is dry, and once at the big trumpet stage—that’s when it matters most. Two sprays: herbicide after emergence, and insecticide for corn borer when I see moths flying.

I’m 70 now. I don’t chase record yields anymore; I chase steady, reliable harvests that my wife and I can bring in without breaking our backs.
